glosses: to fire up, to flare up, to blaze up
внезапно рассердиться, прийти в сильное (обычно кратковременное) раздражение

examples.text: И тут-то, на эти слова, князь вдруг вспылил и начал выкрикивать неприличные слова.

glosses: To ignite.

examples.text: Let's fire up the grill and have a barbecue.

They're[renewables] not strong enough to fire up the plants that you need to make your country great. The wind doesn't blow. Those big windmills are so pathetic and so bad, so expensive to operate, and they have to be rebuilt all the time and they start to rust and rot.

glosses: Of an engine or similar, to start.

examples.text: The generator fired up shortly after the power failure began.

glosses: To launch; to run.

examples.text: Fire up a text editor.
Fire up your computer.

glosses: To excite; to infuse with energy.

examples.text: The band went out to fire up the crowd before the game.

glosses: To grow irritated or angry.

examples.text: He […] fired up, and stood vigorously on his defence.

glosses: To burn brightly again.

examples.text: The fire flared up after we added more wood to it.

glosses: To become more intense suddenly.

examples.text: Reports indicate that tensions have flared up in the Middle East again.
The pain in my shoulder flares up when I turn my head.

glosses: To burst out suddenly, as in anger.

examples.text: The insult made him flare up.
“Well,” I says, “I cal'late a body could get used to Tophet if he stayed there long enough.” ¶ She flared up; the least mite of a slam at Doctor Wool was enough to set her going.
"It's my Welsh half that comes out when I flare up. Let the conjurors take their dirty money and let the rich folk keep their purses shut."

glosses: Alternative form of flare-up.
To travel by airplane to a destination.

examples.text: I'm going to fly out to see you.

glosses: To have someone travel rapidly to a destination on an airplane.

examples.text: flew him out to New York

glosses: To take off from an airfield.

examples.text: Near by is the RAF museum at Duxford Airfield, open at weekends, which has a large display of aircraft. Trapped there is the prototype Concorde, which flew in but can never fly out, because the runway was shortened to make way for a motorway immediately after its arrival.

glosses: To rapidly emerge.

examples.text: Pieces flew out in all directions.

glosses: To become out by hitting a fly ball which is caught.

examples.text: Jones flied out to right field.

glosses: To fly into a rage; to become very angry.
An instance of flying out.

examples.text: A fly out was recorded on the scorecard.

glosses: The visible part of fire; a stream of burning vapour or gas, emitting light and heat.

examples.text: Energy has seldom been found where we need it when we want it. Ancient nomads, wishing to ward off the evening chill and enjoy a meal around a campfire, had to collect wood and then spend time and effort coaxing the heat of friction out from between sticks to kindle a flame.

Long after his cigar burnt bitter, he sat with eyes fixed on the blaze. When the flames at last began to flicker and subside, his lids fluttered, then drooped; but he had lost all reckoning of time when he opened them again to find Miss Erroll in furs and ball-gown kneeling on the hearth[…].

glosses: A romantic partner or lover in a usually short-lived but passionate affair.

examples.text: I could copy out yards of rhapsody to Lord George Poynings, her old flame, in which she addressed him by the most affectionate names.

glosses: An aggressively insulting criticism or remark.

examples.text: Flames are, unfortunately, a fact of USENET life. It's a rare USENET regular who hasn't been shaken to the foundations with anger at something some jerk has posted.

glosses: A brilliant reddish orange-gold fiery colour.

examples.text: [M]arked by myriad clouds of every sunset-colour - flame, purple, pink, green, violet, and all the tints of gold.

flame
The contrasting light and dark figure seen in wood used for stringed instrument making; the curl.

examples.text: The cello has a two-piece back with a beautiful narrow flame.

glosses: Burning zeal, passion, imagination, excitement, or anger.

examples.text: in a flame of zeal severe
where flames refin'd in breasts seraphic glow

Till charming Florio, born to conquer, came
And touch'd the fair one with an equal flame

glosses: A variety of carnation.

examples.text: The Gardeners divide it into Five Claſſes, which they diſtinguiſh by the Name of Picketees, Painted Ladies, Beazarts, Flakes, and Flames: […] the Flames have a red Ground always ſtrip’d with black or very dark Colours.
Sic flow’rs o’ sorts ane seldom sees, / Flecks, flames, bussards an’ picketees, / Wi’ strong carnations, like young trees, / To face the entry; […]

glosses: Of a brilliant reddish orange-gold colour, like that of a flame.
To produce flames; to burn with a flame or blaze.

examples.text: The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing would make it flame again.

glosses: To burst forth like flame; to break out in violence of passion; to be kindled with zeal or ardour.

examples.text: He flamed with indignation.

glosses: To post a destructively critical or abusive message (to somebody).

examples.text: I flamed him for spamming in my favourite newsgroup.

I wish you had the nerve to put your own name on that article, rather than logging into a public account to do it. I would have prefered^([sic]) to respond to you personally, rather than burden the net with my flaming, particularly since opinions like yours are best left ignored. But I feel I must respond to this one.

This was one of the highest points of the show for me. Playin' followed, with a nice jam afterwards. After that, Jerry wandered into Crazy Fingers. (I had been hoping for Terrapin...oh well. Crazy Fingers seems to highlight Jerry's ability to come in late and tentative on lyrics. I'm sure I'll get flamed, since lots of folks seem to worship CF.)
If he got flamed for his lies or his ignorance, he simply moved to another chat room.
Because online communication makes it easy to flame, many of us impetuously fire off messages that we later regret.

glosses: To catch fire and burn until destroyed.

examples.text: Near-synonyms: go up in smoke; see also Thesaurus:combust
The rocket may burn up on reentry.

glosses: To destroy by burning.

examples.text: Before daylight, when the dragon flew home to sleep, he had burned up the hall and even the throne of the Geatish king.

glosses: To anger; to annoy.

examples.text: Near-synonyms: incense; see also Thesaurus:enrage, Thesaurus:annoy
His thoughtlessness really burns me up.

glosses: To be angry or annoyed.

examples.text: One morning […] we stood around the office talking and laughing, having a good time, when one man, Tim, made a job ^([sic]) about "fags." Right then we had to leave, and soon we were warming up our cars on the street. Naturally I was burning up about the comment, and decided to do something about it, though even as I got out of my car to walk up to Tim's, I wasn't sure what.

glosses: To be or feel overly hot or inflamed.

examples.text: Near-synonyms: steam, swelter
It's the middle of summer; I know it's going to be burning up outside.
Now that we've been walking awhile, I'm burning up in this coat! Time to take it off.

glosses: To be or feel overly hot or inflamed.
To experience a high fever.

examples.text: She felt the child's forehead and discovered that he was burning up!

glosses: To ride a motorcycle or other vehicle at high speed.
To use up too much energy when first bowled and to therefore not finishing strongly.
Misspelling of burnup.
S’emporter, s’enflammer.
